title: How a Simple IDOR Earned $5,000 on Reddit
summary_en: An Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in Reddit’s API let an attacker retrieve another user’s data by changing a numeric ID, resulting in a $5,000 bounty.

lesson.example:
**Fictional target:** https://target.example/api/user?id=123
**Vulnerable code (pseudo-Python):**
```python
user_id = request.args.get('id')
# No check that the logged-in user owns this ID
profile = db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s' % user_id)
return json.dumps(profile)
```
**Attack request:**
GET /api/user?id=456 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: session=abcdef

**Why it works:** The server reads the `id` parameter from the URL and directly uses it in the database query without verifying that the requester’s session belongs to that user. Changing `123` to `456` makes the server return another user’s profile (IDOR).

excerpt: Many beginners think that big bounties come from very complex hacking. Often, that is not true. Some of the best-paid bugs come from one small mistake: the server forgot to ask, “Does this really belong to you?” In this article, I explain a real public report from Reddit’s bug bounty program on HackerOne. The report was submitted by a researcher with the username criptex, and the full report is public on HackerOne. The bug was an IDOR, and the reward was $5,000. title: The Art of Escalating Vulnerabilities
summary_en: By chaining a self-XSS with a predictable ID generation algorithm and a WebSocket IDOR, an attacker could inject malicious scripts into any user's chat session to steal API keys and control IoT infrastructure.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by three architectural failures: first, the 'conversationId' was deterministic (predictable) because it was generated using a simple SHA-256 hash of a public username. Second, the WebSocket endpoint lacked authorization checks, allowing any user to connect to any chat ID and send messages. Third, the chat interface failed to sanitize (clean) user-supplied HTML, allowing a 'self-XSS' (a script that only affects the sender) to be upgraded to a 'stored XSS' (a script that affects others) via the IDOR.
lesson.walkthrough: RECON 1. The researcher identified an AI chat widget on an IoT dashboard and tested it for HTML injection (inserting code into a webpage). 2. They sent a basic payload (malicious code) to see if the browser would execute it. Why: This uses an image tag with a broken source ('x') to force the 'onerror' event to run JavaScript. (JavaScript is a programming language used to make websites interactive). DISCOVERY 3. The researcher observed that the chat uses a WebSocket (a persistent two-way connection) to send and receive messages. wss://example.com/api/v1/chatbot?conversationId=chat-app-3f2a9c17d&portal=app Why: This URL contains a 'conversationId' parameter (a unique label for a specific chat) which the researcher suspected could be manipulated. 4. They tested for IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference, where you access data you don't own) by trying to connect to their own chat from a different account. {"type": "user_auth", "user": { "uid": "TARGET_USERNAME" }, "conversationId": "chat-app-3f2a9c17d", "portal": "app"} Why: The server trusted this 'user_auth' packet (a small bundle of data) without checking if the user was actually logged in as that 'uid' (User ID). 5. The researcher looked for how the 'conversationId' was created by searching the site's JavaScript files. generateDeterministicId(userId, portal) { let input = `${userId.toLowerCase()}-${portal.toLowerCase()}`; ... } Why: This code showed that the ID was not random; it was just a hash (a mathematical fingerprint) of the username. 6. They verified they could predict any user's ID by writing a script to mimic the server's logic. def conversation_id(username, portal="app"): return f"chat-{portal}-{hashlib.sha256(data.encode()).hexdigest()[:9]}" Why: This confirmed that knowing a username is enough to calculate their private chat ID offline. 7. They found a way to discover valid usernames using the site's registration check feature. POST /api/user/checkUsername {"username": "testuser1"} Why: This endpoint (a specific web address for a task) tells you if a username exists, allowing an attacker to find targets. EXPLOITATION 8. The researcher combined these findings to send a malicious message to a victim's chat ID using the WebSocket IDOR. ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "chat_message", body: "
lesson.example: Imagine a support site at target.example where your ticket ID is just your 'username' encoded in Base64. If you find a 'self-XSS' in the ticket description field, it seems harmless. However, if the API endpoint 'POST /api/updateTicket' doesn't check if you own the ticket ID you are sending, you can send a request with the Base64 ID of 'admin'. When the admin views their ticket list, your script runs in their browser, potentially stealing their session cookie (a secret file used to keep you logged in).
lesson.takeaway: Always investigate 'Self-XSS' to see if it can be delivered to other users via IDOR or CSRF. If an ID looks like a random string of characters but stays the same every time you log in, check the client-side JavaScript to see if it is 'deterministic' (calculated from public info). Use tools like Burp Suite's 'Comparer' to see how IDs differ between two accounts. A common mistake is assuming that because an ID is a complex hash, it is 'secure'—if the input to the hash is public, the ID is public.

title: Uncovering CVE-2026–105692: Why No Security Flaw Is Too Small to Ignore
summary_en: An IDOR vulnerability in Penpot allowed users with standard editor permissions to delete share-links created by other users, including file owners, disrupting external access.

lesson.cause: The application implemented a 'flat trust model' where any user with a general 'editor' role for a file was granted permission to delete any sub-resource associated with that file. It failed to verify if the authenticated user requesting the deletion was the actual creator or owner of the specific share-link ID being targeted. This authorization gap allowed lower-privileged editors to perform actions that should have been restricted to the resource owner.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Log in to the Penpot platform using an account with standard 'editor' permissions.
User Role: Editor
Why: To establish a baseline of low-privileged access (a user who has permission to be in the system but should have limited control).
DISCOVERY
2. Query the platform to list all active share-links associated with a specific project file.
GET /active-share-links?file_id=TARGET_FILE
Why: To find the unique identifiers for links created by other team members (an HTTP request is a message sent from a browser to a server to ask for data).
3. Identify a Resource ID for a share-link that was generated by a different user, such as the file owner.
Resource ID: [Target Link ID]
Why: This ID is the 'Direct Object Reference' that will be used in the attack (a Resource ID is a unique code used to identify a specific item).
EXPLOITATION
4. Issue a deletion request to the backend using the identified Resource ID of the other user's link.
DELETE /share-link/[Target Link ID]
Why: To test if the server checks who owns the link before deleting it (the backend is the server-side part of the app that handles logic).
IMPACT
5. Observe that the backend executes the request and deletes the link immediately without an ownership check.
Response: 200 OK / Link Deleted
Why: The server incorrectly assumed that any editor could delete any link, leading to an IDOR (a bug where users can change data they do not own).
6. Verify that external stakeholders using that link now receive a 404 error.
HTTP 404 Not Found
Why: The link no longer exists in the database, revoking access without the owner's knowledge (a 404 error is a code meaning a file could not be found).
lesson.example: Imagine a collaborative blog site at target.example where multiple 'Authors' can work on the same project. When an Author creates a 'Preview Link' for a draft, the system assigns it an ID, like 555. If another Author logs in and sends a request to 'DELETE /api/previews/555', a vulnerable system only checks 'Is this user an Author?' rather than 'Did this user create preview 555?'. Because the system only checks the general role and not the specific ownership of the link, the second Author can delete the first Author's work, causing the preview link to break for external editors.
lesson.takeaway: Always test for horizontal privilege escalation in collaborative environments by checking if one user can delete or modify resources created by another user with the same or higher rank. Look for 'flat' permission structures where 'Editor' or 'Member' roles are treated as a single block of trust. Use tools like Burp Suite to capture a deletion request and swap the target ID with one belonging to a different user. A common mistake is assuming that general access to a parent object (like a file) implies total control over all its children (like share-links).
lesson.fix:
The application must implement granular authorization checks that verify resource ownership before performing destructive actions. Instead of just checking if a user has the 'editor' role, the backend should query the database to ensure the 'creator_id' of the specific share-link matches the 'user_id' of the person making the request. If they do not match, the server should return a 403 Forbidden error.

```python
# Fixed Logic Example
link = database.get_share_link(link_id)
if link.creator_id == current_user.id or current_user.is_admin:
    link.delete()
else:
    return "Unauthorized", 403
```

title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR) in Linktree GraphQL API Allows Unauthorized…
summary_en: A Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR) in Linktree’s GraphQL API lets an authenticated user modify a Link belonging to another workspace by swapping the Link ID in a mutation request.

lesson.cause: The server trusts the client‑provided Link identifier without checking that the authenticated user’s workspace owns that Link. The GraphQL resolver for the setDigitalDownloadLinkContext mutation accepts the supplied id and performs the update without verifying the user‑to‑object relationship. Because only authentication is enforced, any valid numeric Link ID can be used to target objects outside the caller’s scope.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1 – Capture a legitimate request
We logged in with a user that can manage its own Links and used the browser’s developer tools to copy the GraphQL request that updates a Link.
Verbatim request line: POST https://graph.linktr.ee/graphql
Why: The POST method sends data to the server; the URL is the GraphQL endpoint.

Step 2 – Identify the object identifier
In the captured request body we saw a field named "id" that held our own Link’s numeric identifier (e.g. <my-authorized-link-id>).
Why: An identifier tells the server which object to modify.

Step 3 – Modify the identifier to another workspace’s ID
We replaced the original id with a known ID from a different workspace (582743627).
Verbatim snippet:
Original Link ID: <my-authorized-link-id>
Modified Link ID: 582743627
Why: Changing the id directs the mutation to a different Link object.

Step 4 – Resend the altered request using the same authenticated session
We sent the edited request back to https://graph.linktr.ee/graphql with the same session cookie.
Why: The server still sees a valid authenticated user, so it processes the mutation.

Step 5 – Observe successful modification
The response indicated the mutation succeeded and the target Link’s fields (title, url, active, status) were updated.
Why: Because the resolver never checked that the user owned the Link, the operation was authorized only by authentication.

EXPLOITATION
Step 6 – Use the setDigitalDownloadLinkContext mutation
The mutation name that performed the change is setDigitalDownloadLinkContext and it accepts fields id, title, url, active, status.
Why: Mutations in GraphQL are the way to change data on the server.

Step 7 – Verify impact
We fetched the modified Link via the public Link URL and saw the new destination URL, confirming a phishing redirect.
Why: Changing the url field controls where visitors are sent.
lesson.takeaway: When testing GraphQL APIs, always look for object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs) in mutation requests. Capture a legitimate request, replace the id with one you have discovered elsewhere, and resend it while keeping the same authentication cookies. Tools such as Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP can automate the replay. Variants of this bug appear in REST endpoints that accept resource IDs in the URL path or JSON body. A common beginner mistake is to assume that being logged in automatically grants permission to edit any object with a valid ID; always verify server‑side ownership checks.

title: The API Was Never Invisible
summary_en: An unauthenticated IDOR in the project‑read endpoint lets any logged‑in user fetch full metadata of another user’s project by supplying an arbitrary projectId, and the file‑upload endpoint permits overwriting a verified document, exposing sensitive data.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a missing ownership check in the GET /v1/sms/onboarding/status/{projectId} endpoint – the server returns project metadata without verifying that the authenticated user owns the projectId. This lack of object‑level access control allows IDOR. The file‑upload flow also lacks integrity checks: the backend accepts a second upload of the same document type and silently overwrites the stored file, because it does not enforce a one‑time‑only rule or validate that the project is still under review. Both flaws stem from trusting client‑side state (project status) instead of re‑checking on the server.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Open the web application in a browser with DevTools open.
Why: DevTools (browser tool) lets us see every network request the frontend makes.
Step 2: Perform every user workflow (onboarding, document upload, etc.) while recording.
Why: Capturing all actions ensures we see all API calls the app uses.
Step 3: Export the captured session as a HAR file (HTTP Archive, a JSON log of requests and responses).
Why: HAR contains URL, method, headers, body, and response for each call.
Step 4: Feed the HAR file to an LLM (Claude) and ask it to list endpoints, methods, parameters, and auth details.
Why: The LLM parses the JSON and produces a readable inventory of the API surface.

DISCOVERY
Step 5: Review the generated inventory and locate the endpoint "GET /v1/sms/onboarding/status/{projectId}".
Why: This endpoint returns project metadata and includes a path parameter {projectId} that can be manipulated.

EXPLOITATION – IDOR
Step 6: Use curl with Account 1’s session cookie to request its own project (baseline).
GET /v1/sms/onboarding/status/12345
Host: api.target.com
Cookie: access_token=AAA; refresh_token=BBB
Why: Baseline shows the normal successful response for a legitimate request.
Step 7: Switch to Account 2’s session cookie and replace the projectId with Account 1’s ID.
GET /v1/sms/onboarding/status/12345
Host: api.target.com
Cookie: access_token=CCC; refresh_token=DDD
Why: If the server does not verify ownership, it returns Account 1’s metadata (IDOR).
Step 8: Observe the response contains Account 1’s name, internal identifier, and timestamps.
Why: This confirms the missing authorization check and data leakage.

EXPLOITATION – FILE UPLOAD OVERWRITE
Step 9: Use curl to upload a valid Word document as the business verification file for Account 1.
[no verbatim request provided in source]
Why: The server accepts the file and stores it on the CDN.
Step 10: While the application is still under review, use curl to upload a second Word document of the same type.
[no verbatim request provided in source]
Why: The backend silently overwrites the original file without changing the database timestamp.
Step 11: Download the file from the CDN and see that the content is the second document.
Why: Overwrite allows an attacker to replace a trusted document with malicious content.

IMPACT
Step 12: Combine the IDOR data with the overwritten document to profile another user and potentially deliver malicious Office files.
Why: Access to another user’s metadata plus a replaceable document creates a privacy and malware risk.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting APIs, always enumerate endpoints that accept an identifier (ID) in the path or query string and test them with a second user’s credentials – this is the classic IDOR pattern. Use HAR files or proxy logs to build a complete map before testing. Tools like Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, or simple curl scripts help automate the cross‑account requests. Variants include missing checks on parent resources (as in the project read endpoint) and indirect IDOR via filtered lists. Beginners often assume a 401 response on a related endpoint means the whole API is safe; always verify each endpoint individually.

title: From Payment Metadata to Unauthorized Subscription Access
summary_en: An unauthenticated API endpoint returns subscription records based on payment metadata, and the returned subscription IDs can be reused in another endpoint to fetch full subscription details, resulting in an access‑control breach.

lesson.cause: The API treats payment‑metadata fields (first six digits, last four digits, expiration date, amount) as an authorization boundary, but these values do not prove ownership of a subscription. The first endpoint returns subscription objects that include a raw identifier ("Id": "sc_...") without checking who is making the request. The second endpoint accepts that identifier as input and returns the full subscription record, again without any ownership or session verification. Because the server never validates that the caller owns the subscription, the identifier becomes an insecure direct object reference (IDOR). The root cause is a missing server‑side ownership/authorization check before exposing subscription data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher sent an unauthenticated request to the lookup endpoint with payment metadata.
{ "firstSix": "424242", "lastFour": "4242", "expDateMonth": 12, "expDateYear": 2030, "amount": 100 }
Why: HTTP request = data sent to a server; JSON payload = structured data; the fields look like card details but no Authorization header, cookie, or token is present, so the server cannot know who is calling.

Step 2: The server responded with a JSON array of subscription objects, each containing an "Id" like "sc_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx".
Why: The response shows that the endpoint returns multiple records; the identifier is a reference to a subscription resource.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: The researcher noted the "Id" field and hypothesised it could be used elsewhere.
Why: In many APIs, a resource ID can be supplied to other endpoints to retrieve more data; this is a typical IDOR pattern.

Step 4: By browsing the API documentation (or fuzzing), the researcher found another endpoint that accepts a subscription ID.
Why: Finding a second endpoint that consumes the same identifier is the key to crossing an authorization boundary.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: The researcher sent an unauthenticated POST request to /subscription/get with the discovered ID.
POST /subscription/get HTTP/1.1\nHost: target.example\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{ "id": "sc_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" }
Why: The request body (payload) supplies the raw ID; no Authorization header or session cookie is included, so the server processes it as any other caller.

Step 6: The server returned the full subscription details (amount, currency, status, next transaction date, etc.).
Why: Because the server trusts the ID without verifying ownership, it leaks sensitive subscription information to anyone who knows the ID.

IMPACT
Step 7: The attacker now has unauthorized access to subscription metadata for many users, including future billing dates and merchant context.
Why: This data exposure can be used for profiling, phishing, or further attacks against the affected merchants and customers.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional service at https://target.example. The API has two endpoints:
1. POST /api/subscriptions/search accepts {"cardBin":"123456","cardLast4":"7890","expMonth":12,"expYear":2025,"amount":50} and returns [{"Id":"sub_abc123","Amount":50,"Status":"Active"}, {"Id":"sub_def456","Amount":75,"Status":"Active"}].
2. POST /api/subscriptions/get accepts {"id":"sub_abc123"} and returns the full record.
If an attacker calls the first endpoint without any auth, they receive the IDs. They then call the second endpoint with one of those IDs, also without auth, and receive the full subscription data. The vulnerability exists because the server never checks that the caller owns "sub_abc123" before returning its details.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting APIs, look for endpoints that return resource identifiers without requiring authentication. Follow those identifiers to other endpoints that accept them as input – this often reveals IDOR or missing access‑control checks. Tools like Burp Suite's Intruder or OWASP ZAP can automate the search for ID parameters. Variants include using order numbers, invoice IDs, or user IDs as keys. A common beginner mistake is to assume that because an endpoint requires "payment metadata" it is safe; always verify that ownership is enforced on every subsequent request.

title: A Simple Question That Led to a Five-Digit Bounty
summary_en: The API returns full customer details for any supplied account_no without verifying the requester’s ownership, resulting in an IDOR information‑disclosure vulnerability.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a missing server‑side authorization check. The backend endpoint /plan_change/Plans/LoginV2Rewamp accepts an "account_no" parameter and returns customer data based solely on that value. No code verifies that the caller owns or is allowed to view the requested account. Because the check is absent, any attacker who can send a request with a different account_no receives that account’s private information. This design flaw turns a legitimate lookup feature into an unrestricted data leak.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the target endpoint. The researcher saw a POST request to /plan_change/Plans/LoginV2Rewamp (an HTTP request is a message a client sends to a server). The request body was JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, a text format for data). 
Why: Knowing the URL and method is the first brick in the attack.

Step 2: Observe the request payload. The JSON contained a single parameter "account_no" (a parameter is a named value the server reads). Example payload:
{
 "account_no": "1234567890"
}
Why: The parameter is the knob the attacker can turn.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Send a valid account_no belonging to the logged‑in user. The server responded with HTTP/1.1 200 OK and a JSON body that included fields like "mobile_num", "email_id", "fullname", and a "token". (HTTP response is the server’s answer; status 200 means success.)
Why: Confirms the endpoint returns personal data.

Step 4: Remove any client‑side checks (the article notes many apps only validate in the browser). The researcher sent the same request without being logged in and still received data.
Why: Shows the server does not enforce authentication.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Change the "account_no" value to another known or guessed identifier (e.g., "9876543210").
Payload:
{
 "account_no": "9876543210"
}
Why: Because the server does not verify ownership, it returns the other account’s details.

Step 6: Repeat with many identifiers to enumerate accounts and harvest names, phone numbers, emails, and authentication tokens.
Why: This is the information‑disclosure impact.

IMPACT
Step 7: Collect the disclosed data. The response includes personally identifiable information (PII) and a token that could be reused elsewhere.
Why: Attackers can use PII for phishing, social engineering, or further attacks.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional service at https://target.example/api/getUser. The server code (pseudo‑code) does:
function getUser(req) {
    var id = req.body.account_no; // reads the supplied parameter
    var user = database.findById(id); // fetches record
    return {status:true, data:user}; // returns everything
}
Because there is no check that req.session.userId == id, any caller can supply any account_no.
Attack request (HTTP POST):
POST https://target.example/api/getUser HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"account_no":"555555"}
The server replies with the full record for account 555555, exposing name, email, phone, etc. The exploit works because the server trusts the supplied identifier without verifying ownership.
lesson.takeaway: When you see an endpoint that returns user data based on an identifier, assume it may lack proper authorization. Look for JSON POST bodies that contain an "id" or "account_no" field and test with values you do not own. Tools like Burp Suite or curl make it easy to replay and modify the payload. Variants of this bug appear in URLs (e.g., /user/123) or in GraphQL queries that accept an ID argument. A common beginner mistake is to assume that a 403 or 401 error means the check is present; many APIs simply return 200 with empty data, which can still be abused if the check is missing.

title: How I got my first $13500 bounty through Parameter Polluting (HPP)
summary_en: An HPP/logic flaw in a housing site's registration let the researcher create a host account without a valid host ID, unlocking 4 privileged features. Chaining a public 3-character IDOR (leaking confidential form data) with a self-XSS turned it into reflected XSS — $13,500 in bounties.
summary_ar: خلل منطقي (HPP) في تسجيل موقع إسكان خلّى الباحث ينشئ حساب host من غير ID صالح، ففتح له 4 ميزات محمية. وبسلسلة IDOR عام من 3 حروف (تسريب بيانات سرية) مع self-XSS حوّلها لـ reflected XSS — مجموع الـ bounties $13,500.

lesson.cause_ar: السبب الجذري خلل منطقي في تسجيل الحسابات: السيرفر كان بيقرر إن المستخدم host ولا customer بناءً على وجود باراميتر HostId في الطلب، لكنه كان بيتحقق من صحة الـ HostId فقط لما يكون IsHost=1. النتيجة إن أي حد يقدر يبعت IsHost=0&HostId=123 فيتحول حسابه إلى host من غير أي تحقق من صحة الـ ID. ده فتح 4 ميزات محمية خلف دور الـ host، وكلها كانت مبنية على افتراض إن اللي وصلها host حقيقي. وبعدين الميزات نفسها كانت ناقصة الـ authorization checks: الـ form كان بياخد ID عام من 3 حروف بدون أي حماية، والـ file upload كان بيدي لينك منفصل قابل للتعداد. حتى الـ XSS كانت self-XSS في البداية، لكن الـ IDOR حوّلها إلى reflected XSS لأن الاسم كان بينعكس في صفحة الـ form العامة.
lesson.walkthrough_ar:
الخطوة 1: الباحث كان بيفحص موقع إسكان (housing) معمول من موقع رئيسي فيه نوعين حسابات (host/customer) و subdomain فيه sub-service بياخد بيانات من الموقع الرئيسي.
الخطوة 2: في نموذج التسجيل بتختار إنك host أو customer وبتدخل الـ ID بتاعك، والموقع المفروض يتحقق إن الـ ID صالح ويجيب معلوماتك.
الخطوة 3: لاحظ حاجة غريبة: قسم الـ hosting معطل تمامًا — مهما كان الـ ID صالح بيقولك invalid أو مش قادر يجيب المعلومات.
الخطوة 4: استنتج إن مفيش صياد ثغرات قبله قدر يعمل host account، وإن اللي ورا القسم ده لسه مستكشف.
الخطوة 5: شكل طلب التسجيل لما تختار host:
IsHost=1&HostId=123&Email=test%40test.com
الخطوة 6: وشكل الطلب لما تختار customer:
IsHost=0&Email=test%40test.com
(لاحظ: مفيش HostId خالص في حالة customer)
الخطوة 7: فكّر في الـ logic اللي شغال ورا الكواليس ولقاه:
- لو HostId موجود و IsHost=1 → دوّر على الـ hostID وفشل.
- لو HostId مش موجود و IsHost=0 → user عادي وكمّل.
- لو HostId موجود و IsHost=0 → user هو host بس من غير ما يدور على الـ hostID (!!).
الخطوة 8: يعني السيرفر بيحدد إنك host من وجود الـ HostId نفسه، لكنه بيعمل التحقق من صحته بس لما IsHost=1.
الخطوة 9: فبعت طلب تسجيل بالشكل ده:
IsHost=0&HostId=123&Email=test%40test.com
الخطوة 10: النتيجة: اتفتح له حساب host صالح بدون أي تحقق من الـ ID — وده جوهر الـ HPP/الخلل المنطقي.
الخطوة 11: الحساب ده فتح له 4 ميزات جديدة، وبدأ يفحصها واحدة واحدة.
الخطوة 12: واحدة من الميزات كانت form submission فيه بيانات سرية (بيانات المستخدم + بيانات جاية من الموقع الرئيسي).
الخطوة 13: لما بتقدم الـ form بيجيلك ID فريد من 3 حروف في الـ URL بيفتح الـ form بتاعك.
الخطوة 14: الـ ID ده public وبدون أي حماية → IDOR عام: تقدر تشوف forms ناس تانية، وتقدر تبعت رابط لضحية لو لقيت XSS.
الخطوة 15: كل الـ inputs كانت sanitized صح ومفيش XSS مباشر — بس كان ليه finding قديم: حقل الاسم فيه XSS، لكن الاسم خاص بيه وحده → self-XSS.
الخطوة 16: الـ chain: الاسم بينعكس في الـ form وفي صفحة الـ 3 حروف، فبفضل الـ IDOR الـ self-XSS اتقلبت reflected XSS — يبعت الرابط للضحية والـ payload يشتغل في سياقها.
الخطوة 17: الـ form كان فيه file upload بيدي لينك منفصل للملف، واللينك ده كان vulnerable لوحده — تقدر تشوف ملفات ناس تانية (IDOR تاني).
الخطوة 18: النتيجة النهائية: Main IDOR بـ $12000 (critical لأن البيانات جاية من الموقع الرئيسي)، File IDOR بـ $1000، و XSS بـ $500 — المجموع $13500.
lesson.takeaway_ar: دور على النمط ده في أي تسجيل أو تغيير دور: لو في باراميتر بيحدد الدور (IsHost, role, type) وباراميتر تاني بيتحقق منه بشكل مشروط، جرّب تفصل بينهم — ابعت الدور customer والـ ID موجود، أو ابعت نفس الباراميتر مرتين (HPP). العلامة الذهبية: لما ميزة معينة تكون معطلة للكل (زي قسم الـ hosting هنا) يبقى غالبًا وراها logic غلط ومفيش حد كشفها. كمان أي ID قصير أو sequential في الـ URL (3 حروف، أرقام صغيرة) يستاهل تجربة enumeration فورًا. ولو لقيت self-XSS متستهونش بيه — دوّر على أي مكان بينعكس فيه الاسم/البيانات دي في صفحة عامة أو قابلة للمشاركة عشان ترفعه لـ reflected. وأخيرًا اختبر الـ file upload links كأهداف مستقلة مش كجزء من الـ form.

excerpt: This write-up is about 2 IDORs and an XSS I found on a housing website. However what led me into these bugs is the point of this article. title: The Butterfly Effect: Turning Overlooked Misconfigurations into Zero Click Account Takeover
summary_en: A chain of overlooked GraphQL misconfigurations — enabled suggestions, an IDOR that enumerated students and admins, and a login mutation that accepted an empty password when loggedSSO=true — escalated into zero-click takeover of any account on an e-learning platform.
summary_ar: سلسلة من سوء الإعدادات في GraphQL — تفعيل الـ suggestions، وثغرة IDOR لسرد الطلاب والمشرفين، وmutation تسجيل دخول تقبل كلمة مرور فارغة عند تمرير loggedSSO=true — تحوّلت إلى استيلاء كامل (zero-click) على أي حساب في منصة تعليم إلكتروني.

lesson.cause_ar: السبب الجذري ليس ثغرة واحدة بل سلسلة إعدادات خاطئة تراكمت فوق بعضها. أولاً، خاصية GraphQL suggestions كانت مفعّلة في بيئة الإنتاج، فسرّبت أسماء الـ queries والـ mutations المتاحة للمهاجم. ثانيًا، الـ resolvers الخاصة بـ student(id) و administrator(id) كانت ترجع بيانات أي كائن بمجرد تمرير الـ id من غير أي تحقق أن المستخدم الحالي يملك صلاحية الوصول لهذا الكائن — غياب تام للـ object-level authorization. ثالثًا — والأخطر — الـ backend الخاص بـ loginStudent لم يفرض فعليًا القيد non-nullable على حقل password رغم أن الـ schema يعرّفه بعلامة !، وكان تمرير loggedSSO=true يختصر التحقق من كلمة المرور بالكامل. وأخيرًا، توكن المشرف كان يتطلب claim إضافي اسمه adminLevel داخل الـ JWT، وهذا الـ claim كان متاحًا عبر ثغرة الـ IDOR. كل عنصر لوحده يبدو منخفض الخطورة، لكنه معًا شكّل سلسلة استيلاء كامل على الحسابات.
lesson.walkthrough_ar:
الخطوة 1: السياق — الباحث كان في اختبار اختراق لمنصة تعليم إلكتروني للطلاب (تطوير داخلي) أثناء ترحيلها من مزوّد استضافة خارجي إلى بيئة سحابية جديدة، والهدف foo.target.com. ليه: التطبيقات المطوّرة داخليًا غالبًا مليانة إعدادات مهملة، والترحيل فرصة ذهبية لظهور أخطاء.
الخطوة 2: أثناء رسم خريطة التطبيق اكتشف أن الـ API مبني على GraphQL. ليه: GraphQL يسمح بطلب بيانات محددة بدقة، وسوء إعداده يفتح أبوابًا كثيرة.
الخطوة 3: لاحظ أن خاصية GraphQL suggestions مفعّلة في الإنتاج، فبدأت تقترح عليه الـ queries والـ mutations المتاحة. ليه: تسريب بنية الـ schema يساعد المهاجم في صياغة هجمات أدق.
الخطوة 4: اكتشف IDOR في query باسم student — بجلسة طالب عادية استطاع سرد بيانات أي طالب عبر تغيير الـ id. الطلب:
POST /graphql
Host: foo.target.com
Authorization: Bearer [Student JWT]
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "operationName": "student",
  "variables": {},
  "query": "query student {\n  student(id:1234) {\n    firstName\n    lastName\n    profile\n    affiliation\n    email\n    createdAt\n    __typename\n  }\n}"
}
الاستجابة رجعت بيانات Alan Turing كاملة (email و affiliation و profile). ليه: الـ resolver بيرجع بيانات أي id من غير ما يتحقق إن الطالب صاحب الجلسة هو نفسه صاحب الـ id.
الخطوة 5: نفس الفكرة مع administrator(id:500) — سرد بيانات المشرفين ومنها adminLevel و trainerId. الاستجابة رجعت بيانات Linus Torvalds مع adminLevel: 2. ليه: نفس غياب الـ authorization على مستوى الـ object.
الخطوة 6: حلّل ملفات JavaScript الخاصة بالتطبيق ووجد mutation باسم loginStudent فيها email و password و loggedSSO وكلها معلمة بعلامة ! (non-nullable). ليه: ملفات الـ JS بتسرّب بنية الـ API الداخلية.
الخطوة 7: جرّب تمرير loggedSSO: true مع إيميل طالب وبدون تعيين كلمة المرور — فوجئ بأن السيرفر أعاد access token للطالب. ليه: الـ backend ما فرضش الـ non-null رغم تعريف الـ schema، وflag الـ loggedSSO اختصر التحقق من كلمة المرور.
الخطوة 8: الطلب النهائي للاستيلاء على حساب طالب:
POST /graphql
Host: foo.target.tld
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "operationName": "LoginStudent",
  "variables": {
    "email": "alan.turing@student.tld",
    "password": "",
    "loggedSSO": true
  },
  "query": "mutation LoginStudent($email: String, $uid: String, $password: String, $loggedSSO: Boolean!, $dataToUpdate: String) {\n  loginStudent(\n    email: $email\n    uid: $uid\n    password: $password\n    loggedSSO: $loggedSSO\n    dataToUpdate: $dataToUpdate\n  )\n}"
}
الاستجابة رجعت JWT يخص الطالب. ليه: كلمة المرور الفارغة مرّت لأن التحقق الفعلي مشغّل على الـ loggedSSO مش على الـ password.
الخطوة 9: بدمج الـ IDOR مع الـ bypass بقدر ياخد أي حساب طالب بإيميله فقط. ليه: الـ IDOR وفّر قائمة الإيميلات والـ bypass وفّر الدخول.
الخطوة 10: جرّب نفس الأسلوب بإيميل مشرف — حصل على session token لكنه ما قدرش يستخدم مزايا المشرف. ليه: توكن المشرف لازم يحوي claim إضافي اسمه adminLevel داخل جسم الـ JWT.
الخطوة 11: عرف من نتيجة الـ IDOR إن الـ adminLevel بيرجع مع بيانات المشرف (مثلاً adminLevel: 2). ليه: الـ claim ده هو اللي بيميّز صلاحيات المشرف.
الخطوة 12: حاول فرض adminLevel في الطلب لكن بدون نجاح. ليه: السيرفر مش بيقبل claim مفروض من العميل.
الخطوة 13: جرّب تغيير الـ mutation إلى LoginAdmin — فظهرت رسالة خطأ من GraphQL suggestions: Cannot query field "LoginAdmin" on type "Mutation". Did you mean "loginAdmin" or "signupAdmin"? ليه: الـ suggestions كشفت الاسم الصحيح للـ mutation.
الخطوة 14: استخدم loginAdmin بنفس منطق loggedSSO=true وبدون كلمة مرور — نجح bypass لصلاحيات المشرف. ليه: نفس الخلل في التحقق من كلمة المرور موجود في mutation تسجيل دخول المشرف، فاكتملت السلسلة من IDOR إلى استيلاء كامل على حساب مشرف.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أول ما تشوف GraphQL في هدف، جرّب فورًا الـ introspection والـ suggestions — لو رجّعوا أسماء عمليات، دي إشارة قوية إن الـ schema مسرّب. دوّر في ملفات الـ JS على أسماء mutations خاصة بالدخول، وابحث عن أي parameter من نوع flag (زي loggedSSO أو isSSO أو rememberMe) ممكن يختصر التحقق. قارن دايماً بين تعريف الـ schema (علامة !) والسلوك الفعلي للـ backend — التناقض بينهم كنز حقيقي. ولو لقيت IDOR في query بيرجّع بيانات مستخدمين، استخدمه لبناء قائمة أهداف ثم ادمجه مع أي bypass للدخول. الفكرة الكبرى: ثغرة low severity مش نهاية القصة، جرّب تركّبها مع غيرها.

excerpt: In the world of application security, even low severity misconfigurations can act as a butterfly’s wing flap, triggering a chain reaction that leads to more impactful attack scenarios. Along the way, you’ll see how every overlooked detail and misconfiguration can become a stepping stone for a determined attacker.
